PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 6

Animals & Their Sounds

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 6Subjects Animals & their sounds

Twelve animal friends on twelve picture cards — a dog, a cat, a cow, a sheep, a duck, a chicken, a horse, a pig, a lion, an elephant, a frog and a bird. Hear real animal sounds, guess who is hiding behind each one, match animals to their voices and take the whole farmyard off screen: this class follows Opposites & Comparing on the preschool path.

Animal sounds are the first words many children read — a woof or a moo is a word your child can say perfectly, right now. Say every sound together, make them loud and make them silly, and let the animal do the talking.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, little one on the lap or stomping like an elephant — both work.
TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Here’s how class goes: say hi, meet the animals, listen to their real sounds, do the animal sheets, then get up and play. You can do the steps in any order. Stop whenever you want, because stopping still counts as a whole class. Nobody is keeping score.

  1. 1 Teacher welcome
  2. 2 Meet the animals
  3. 3 Listen: hear the sounds
  4. 4 Solve the sheets
  5. 5 Take it off screen
  6. 6 Class complete
TEACHER WELCOME

“Hello, my friend! Guess what? Today our classroom is a barnyard. We’re going to meet twelve animal friends, listen to their real sounds, and make every one of those sounds ourselves. Woof! Moo! Roar! Ready? Let’s go!”

— Your Kiddo School teacher

Begin the class ↓First stop: the animal cards. Or jump straight to the sounds below.
MEET THE ANIMALS

Twelve animal friends.

Say each animal’s name when you see it. Then make its sound! Your woof can sound however you like. Tap the arrows to go card by card, or just scroll down. All twelve are waiting.

Card 1 of 12
Or simply scroll: all 12 cards are below.

Say the sounds together

  • Farm friends first. Woof, meow, moo, baa, quack, cluck, neigh, oink! Those are the sounds you’d hear all day on a farm.
  • Now the wild ones. Roar, toot (that’s the elephant), ribbit and tweet! Big voices from the jungle, the pond and the trees outside your window.
LISTEN · HEAR THE SOUNDS

Press play, then press it again.

These are real animals! Tap play and listen. Then say the sound back in your own voice, as big as you can. Want to hear it again? Tap it again. Playing it over and over is the fun part.

The duck, the elephant and the frog are on the cards above, and their recordings are on the way — until then, you make the quack, the trumpet and the ribbit yourself. You’re probably better at it anyway.

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the animal sheets together.

Print the twelve animal cards and they turn into your worksheets. Cut them out, say each name, and you’re ready to play.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twelve, two to a page. Cut them out, and say each animal’s name as you cut.

  2. 02

    Say the sound

    Pick a card, hold it up and make its sound. Woof! Moo! Tweet! Silly sounds count double.

  3. 03

    Act the animal out

    Walk like a dog, waddle like a duck, stomp like an elephant. Can somebody guess which animal you are?

  4. 04

    Match card to world

    Put three cards on the table and find the same animals in a picture book. Then color your favorite card with the Write & Color tool.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

OFF-SCREEN PLAY

Be the animal.

Time to get up and be the animals! It’s loud, it’s wiggly, and you can’t get it wrong. Pick one game. Two minutes is plenty.

Old MacDonald, live from your kitchen

  • Pick any three animals from your cards and sing their verse. “Old MacDonald had a farm, and on that farm he had a… dog!” Then you choose the next animal and make its sound.

Move like the animal

  • Pick a card and move like the animal. Gallop like a horse, waddle like a duck, prowl like a lion, hop like a frog. Take turns: one of you picks the animal, and the other one moves.

Sound walk

  • Next time you go outside, listen for real animals. A dog on a porch? Birds in the trees? When you hear one, say its name and make its sound.

Zoo box guess

  • Put two or three animal toys (or animal cards) in a box. One player hides an animal and makes its sound. The other player reaches in and finds the right one, just by listening.

Stop when it stops being fun. There’s nothing to finish.

PRINT THE CARDS

Take the animals to the kitchen table!

Print all twelve cards, two to a page. Cut them out and you can play with the whole set on the table.

View Printable Cards ↗

Stick them on the fridge or your bedroom door. You can also find the same cards in the animal flashcards.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Sound play is language practice wearing a costume: every woof your child makes exercises the same listening, breath control and word-making skills that sentences need later. If your child repeats one sound forty times, that is not a hiccup — that is the lesson working. The recordings here are real animals, but your voice is the one that counts: play the sound once, then answer it in your own voice so your child can copy a human.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Play the sound once, then answer it yourself: the recording catches attention, your voice teaches. Say the animal’s name and its sound together — “dog… woof!” — and give your child the tap in every game, even when the answer looks obvious to you. The finger teaches the ear.

Then hand the class over: your child presses play and YOU guess. Getting one wrong on purpose — “a cow says tweet!” — keeps the game alive for weeks, and being the quiz master is powerful practice for a three-year-old.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class was one big woof and one bigger roar, today’s class was a success.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Dog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts the animal-sound collection with the voice your child already knows best. Woof is more than a fun noise — it is our word for a dog’s bark, and learning it means learning how people copy the sounds animals make.

    What is this?

    A dog is a four-legged friend who lives with people — a pet that eats, plays, naps and greets the whole family at the door. When a dog makes its loud voice, we write it as woof: that is our word for the bark, our copy of the real thing.

    What does it mean?

    Here is the honest part: a dog does not know the word woof. Barking is the dog’s true voice — short, loud, repeated — and people listened and made a word that sounds like it. In English that word is woof. Every language built its own copy, but the bark they are all imitating is the same one.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs three things: a dog’s sound is called woof in English, real dogs bark for reasons — hello, warning, excitement — and a dog we meet belongs to somebody, so we ask the person before we stroke the dog.

    Why this matters

    Animal sounds are a child’s first matching game: sound to animal, animal to word. Getting woof right trains listening and memory, hands over a proud piece of knowledge, and unlocks every dog story on the shelf — because now your child can supply the voice.

    What it teaches

    Listening and matching, sound imitation — real practice for strong consonants — animal vocabulary, empathy for living creatures, and the social rule of asking before touching someone else’s pet.

    Words to learn

    dogwoofbarkpuppypetgentle

    Say this to your child

    “"The dog says woof! Woof woof! A bark is the dog’s big voice, and woof is our word for it — the sound people hear when a dog talks. Can you say woof? Loud woof, soft woof, fast woof, slow woof — you speak dog!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask the big question first: what does the dog say? Let the woof come from your child if it can — owning the answer beats hearing it.
    2. Say the pair in one breath — the dog says woof — then answer each other: you woof, your child woofs back, a whole conversation with a single word.
    3. Look at the picture together: a happy brown puppy. Ask what the puppy might be woofing about — dinner? a walk? a ball under the sofa?
    4. Play sound match: line up three or four animal cards, make one sound, and let your child grab the animal that owns it.
    5. Set the real-world rule gently: when we meet a dog on its lead, we ask its person first, then stroke softly on the back. Rule and sound, learned in one lesson.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the puppy? Is it sitting or standing? Does its face look happy or cross? Where is the word dog written?

    Ask your child

    "What does the dog say?" "Why do you think the puppy looks happy?" "What do we do before we stroke a real dog?" "Can you woof softly, like a puppy falling asleep?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may answer every dog story with a full-volume woof, match the sound to the card in one grab, or rehearse the asking rule aloud — "may I stroke your dog?" — ready for the next walk.

    Out in the real world

    Dogs bark all over town: behind garden fences, in the park, on television, at the door when friends arrive. Each bark you hear is a round of the matching game — "whose voice was that?" — and your child already knows the answer.

    Try it together

    Sound match backwards: spread three or four animal cards face up. You make a sound — woof! — and your child grabs the right card. Then swap: your child makes the sound, you point, and get one wrong on purpose. Being corrected by a three-year-old is the best reward this game has.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the dog say? What do we ask before stroking a dog? Show me a soft woof." The bark, the rule and the whisper — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The sound is the easy half and the name is the other half — keep both in every round: dog, woof; woof, dog. If your child answers everything with woof for a few days, that is normal: fresh words get used like hammers. Let the woof run its course.

    Staying safe

    Real dogs are stroked only with their person’s permission — ask first, let the dog sniff a hand, then touch gently on the back, away from the face, the tail and the food bowl. A dog that is eating or sleeping gets left alone.

    This lesson pairs with the Dog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Cat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson brings the softest voice in the collection indoors. Meow is our copy of a cat’s call — long, stretchy, a little demanding — and the kitten on the card is sitting up, ready to demonstrate it in your child’s best voice.

    What is this?

    A cat is a small, soft pet with quick feet, sharp ears and a quiet way of walking. When a cat lifts its head and calls, people copy the sound as meow: a long, stretchy word for a long, stretchy voice.

    What does it mean?

    The meow on the card is a people-word, not the cat’s own name for its call. And here is a fact worth sharing: grown-up cats save meow mostly for humans — with each other they sniff, rub and purr far more than they meow. The call is how a cat talks to us, which makes your child the exact audience for it.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: a cat’s sound is written meow in English, cats purr when they are content — a rumbly second voice — and they move on quiet feet. Cats we do not know are looked at, not grabbed; the asking rule from the dog works here too.

    Why this matters

    Meow is the perfect first stretchy sound: it slides, it holds, it can be loud or tiny. Copying it exercises the voice muscles that speech needs, and the quiet-cat games build the body control that circle time will one day call sitting nicely.

    What it teaches

    Voice modulation (stretching, whispering, squeaking a single word), imitation and listening, animal vocabulary, gentle-hands practice, and the self-control of moving slowly and softly on purpose.

    Words to learn

    catmeowkittenpurrsoftquiet

    Say this to your child

    “"The cat says meow! Meee-ow — stretch it out long, like a ribbon. Meow is our word for the cat’s call, and cats mostly say it to people — to you! Can you purr too? Rrrrr. Two cat sounds in one lesson: the loud one and the rumbly one."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the kitten is saying. Collect every guess, then model it: meee-ow, long and slow.
    2. Say the pair together — the cat says meow — and stretch the word across the whole breath. Long meow, short meow, squeaky meow: the word is a toy.
    3. Look at the picture: an orange kitten sitting up. Ask what a sitting kitten might be asking for — dinner? a door opened? a lap?
    4. Try the purr next: a low rrrrumble in the throat. It is the cat’s second sound, and children are surprisingly good at it.
    5. Set the rule for real cats: ask the person nearby first, then let the cat come to you. A cat that walks away has answered too.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the kitten? Is it sitting or moving? Where are its ears pointing? What word sits under the kitten?

    Ask your child

    "What does the cat say?" "Why do you think cats walk so quietly?" "What sound does a happy cat make instead?" "What do we do before touching a cat we do not know?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may meow at every cat picture for a week, purr on request with alarming realism, or creep across the floor on silent feet announcing "quiet cat coming through!" — the sound and the walk arriving as a set.

    Out in the real world

    Cats appear on fences, in windows, in storybooks and in the neighbour’s garden. Every one is a chance to whisper-meow together and ask the big question — what is that cat saying? — with the whole street as the practice field.

    Try it together

    Quiet-cat creep: music on, everyone struts like lions — then the music stops and the cats take over: slow steps, soft feet, meows in whispers only. The moment somebody stomps, the dogs win. It is volume control wearing a costume.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the cat say? What is the rumbly sound? How do we move like a cat?" The stretched meow, the purr and the silent creep — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Accept every meow volume — the point is the stretch, not the loudness. And if your child meows instead of answering you for a day, play along: asking the cat questions back keeps the game alive and the talking going, which is the whole point of talking at all.

    Staying safe

    Cats we do not know are watched, not grabbed — ask the person nearby first, and let the cat choose to come close. Never touch a cat that hisses, flattens its ears or backs away; those are the cat’s words for not-yet.

    This lesson pairs with the Cat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Cow — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes the biggest voice in the barnyard and gives it room. Moo is long, low and lazy — and while your child is enjoying it, the sound is quietly teaching slow, controlled breathing that speech and singing will use for years.

    What is this?

    A cow is a big farm animal with kind eyes, a spotted coat and a voice to match its size. The call goes out slow and rumbly, and people copied it as moo — one of the oldest animal words there is, and one of the easiest to say big.

    What does it mean?

    A cow says moo because that is how people hear it. The real call is a long, low rumble from deep in the chest; moo is our mouth’s best copy of that rumble. Say moo slowly and you can feel the shape of the true sound: wide open, low, in no hurry at all.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the cow’s sound is written moo in English, cows give us milk, and cows call to their calves and to the farmer with that big slow voice. Moo is made with a wide-open mouth and a long breath — the body knows it before the word does.

    Why this matters

    Moo is the best breath exercise disguised as a game. Holding a long, low sound takes controlled air — the same control behind singing, long sentences and calm-down breathing. Every giant moo is oral-motor training that feels like pure silliness.

    What it teaches

    Breath control and sustained voicing, pitch play (high moos, deep moos), animal and farm vocabulary, the cause-and-effect of milk coming from cows, and confident loudness — a safe place to be huge.

    Words to learn

    cowmoofarmmilklowherd

    Say this to your child

    “"The cow says moo! Mooooo — open wide, start low, and let it rumble all the way out. Moo is our word for the cow’s big slow call. Can you make the longest moo in the house? And guess what — the milk in our fridge came from a cow just like this one."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask who this big spotted animal might be. Then ask the question the farm answers: what does it say? Take any guess, then give the real one.
    2. Say the pair — the cow says moo — and make your best long, low moo together. Slow is the rule: a moo that lasts the whole breath.
    3. Look at the picture: a farm cow, spotted black and white. Run a finger over the spots and name the colors — black, white, black, white.
    4. Form a kitchen barnyard choir: everyone moos at their own pitch — squeaky moos, deep moos, slow moos — and votes on the most cow-ish one.
    5. Connect the milk: we drink milk at breakfast, and milk comes from cows. The carton in the fridge is the proof your child can hold.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what colors are the spots? Where is the cow looking? What word sits with the cow? Does the cow look big or little?

    Ask your child

    "What does the cow say?" "Where does our milk come from?" "Can you make a deep, slow moo — the biggest one you have?" "What sound would a baby cow make?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may fill entire car journeys with moos, answer the milk-carton question with pride, or line up the animal cards and give the cow the deepest voice of all — the big animal, the big sound, correctly matched.

    Out in the real world

    Cows graze in fields on the drive out of town, appear at farms and county fairs, and stand on every milk carton in the fridge. Each sighting earns its moo — and each carton at breakfast is a quiet repeat of where milk really comes from.

    Try it together

    The barnyard choir: assign everyone an animal — you the sheep, your child the cow, a teddy the duck — and sing a verse of a familiar tune, but each singer may only make their animal’s sound. The cow carries the low part. It is a concert, a matching game and a breath workout in one.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the cow say? Where does milk come from? Make your longest moo." The long, low rumble, the answer and the wide-open mouth — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Judge the moo contest generously and often — longest, deepest, slowest — because every round is another slow-breath exercise. And when the moos migrate to the supermarket, let them: a cow sound in public is a small price for a word this well loved.

    Staying safe

    If you visit real cows at a farm or a field, admire them from the fence — big animals get big space, and feeding happens only when the farmer hands out the job.

    This lesson pairs with the Cow flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Sheep — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gathers the flock. Baa is short with a wobble on the end — a sound children find irresistible — and the fluffy sheep on the card comes with a bonus story: where jumpers, hats and blankets begin.

    What is this?

    A sheep is a woolly farm animal that lives in a flock with its friends. Its call is short with a tremble at the finish, and people copied it as baa — baa-aa-aa — with the wobble built right into the word.

    What does it mean?

    Baa is our copy of a sheep’s call, wobble included. The wobble is real: a sheep’s voice trembles as the sound fades, which is why our word ends in a waver too. Copying the wobble is the fun part — and it takes more voice control than your child expects.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the sheep’s sound is written baa in English, sheep wear coats of wool that keep them warm, and people cut the wool gently and turn it into warm things — jumpers, hats, blankets. The sheep stay together as a flock, and so do their baas.

    Why this matters

    The wobble in baa is a mini voice lesson: fading a sound out slowly is harder and more valuable than switching it off. And the flock idea — sheep sticking together, baas coming in groups — is social learning dressed as animal facts.

    What it teaches

    Voice control (starting, wobbling, fading a sound), rhythm and bouncing movement, animal and clothing vocabulary connected by one material — wool — and the togetherness feeling of making a sound as a group.

    Words to learn

    sheepbaawoolflockfluffywobble

    Say this to your child

    “"The sheep says baa! Baa-aa-aa — hear the wobble at the end? That is our copy of the sheep’s real call, wobble and all. Sheep wear coats of wool — the softest coats on the farm — and they stay together in a flock. Shall we be a flock? One, two, three: BAA!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the fluffy animal says. Then give the full version, wobble included: baa-aa-aa.
    2. Say the pair — the sheep says baa — and practise the wobble: start the baa strong and let it tremble away to nothing.
    3. Look at the picture: a white, fluffy sheep. Feel something fluffy nearby — a blanket, a teddy, a woolly hat — and say: a sheep wears a coat like this.
    4. Follow the wool story: the sheep’s coat gets a haircut, the wool gets washed and spun, and it comes back as a jumper. Find one woolly thing in the house as the exhibit.
    5. Make a flock: everyone in the family baas at once, wobbling together. A flock is exactly this — sheep staying together, in voice and in walking.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the sheep? Does its coat look smooth or fluffy? What word sits with the sheep? Is the sheep alone on the card or with friends?

    Ask your child

    "What does the sheep say?" "Where does your woolly jumper begin?" "Why do sheep stay in a flock?" "Can your baa wobble at the end like a real sheep?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may baa in a wobbling whisper at bedtime, trace the family tree of a woolly hat back to a sheep with enormous pride, or organize the whole family into a bleating flock — leadership, wool economics and phonics in one game.

    Out in the real world

    Sheep appear on hillsides and at petting farms, and wool appears on every coat hook in the house. The trail from field to jumper is one of the first make-it stories a child can fully follow — start it at the hat rack.

    Try it together

    The flock game: everyone walks in a loose circle, and when you call flock! all the sheep must baa together and huddle into one woolly group. Call stray sheep! and one sheep wanders off — the flock has to baa louder until it comes back. Togetherness has never been noisier.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the sheep say? What do we make from its coat? Show me a baa with a wobble." The fading wobble, the jumper and the group baa — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Practise the wobble on long vowels your child already has — ahh-aa-aa — before adding the b. And keep the flock game short: three rounds of group bleating is charming, thirty is a decision you will regret at bedtime.

    This lesson pairs with the Sheep flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Duck — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes to the water. Quack is short, sharp and made for shouting — and the card holds a secret worth telling: the yellow bird on it is a duckling, a baby duck, and baby ducks do not quack yet at all.

    What is this?

    A duck is a water bird with flat feet, a flat bill and a body built for paddling. When grown-up ducks call across the pond, people copy the sound as quack: short, sharp, over and over, like a conversation you can count.

    What does it mean?

    Quack is our copy of the duck’s call. And here is the secret on the card: the bird pictured is a duckling — a baby duck — and ducklings peep instead of quacking. The peep grows into the quack as the duck grows up, exactly the way your child’s voice is growing too.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the duck’s sound is written quack in English, a baby duck is a duckling and says peep, ducks paddle on water with flat feet, and real ducks are chatty — a pond is full of quack conversations.

    Why this matters

    The duckling secret teaches something big in a small package: animals have babies, and babies change. A child who can explain that the duckling will grow into its quack has grasped growing-up itself — and will apply it to kittens, puppies and, sooner or later, themselves.

    What it teaches

    Animal family vocabulary (duck, duckling), the concept of baby animals changing as they grow, rhythm and counting in the waddle games, imitation of a short sharp sound, and pond-side observation skills.

    Words to learn

    duckquackducklingpondbillpaddle

    Say this to your child

    “"The duck says quack! Quack, quack — short and sharp, like the duck is laughing! And the baby on our card is a duckling: peep, peep! The peep grows into the quack as the duckling grows up. Can you do baby duck and big duck? Peep… QUACK!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the little yellow bird says. Accept quack — then spring the secret: this is a duckling, and ducklings say peep!
    2. Make both sounds: the tiny peep of the baby and the big sharp quack of the grown-up. Your child just learned the whole duck life story in two noises.
    3. Say the pair — the duck says quack — and make it staccato: quack, quack, quack, like laughter with feathers.
    4. Waddle together: flat feet, side-to-side sway, two steps and a quack, two steps and a quack. Ducks walk like this because of where their legs sit.
    5. Visit real ducks if there is a pond nearby: sit at a distance, watch the paddling feet, and count the quacks together. Feeds bread? Leave it at home — ducks do their best with their own pond food.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the little bird? Does it look big or small — grown-up or a baby? What word sits with it? Where would a bird like this go swimming?

    Ask your child

    "What does the duck say?" "What does the baby duck say instead?" "How does a duckling grow into a quack?" "How do ducks walk — show me!"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may quack every morning for a week, explain the peep-to-quack story to anyone who stands still, or waddle down the hallway flat-footed and proud — sound, walk and baby-secret all on display.

    Out in the real world

    Ducks live at nearly every park pond, and ducklings follow their mother in spring in a line your child will never forget. Quacks drift up from the water all year — each one a round of name-that-sound.

    Try it together

    Waddle-and-quack parade: the whole family lines up behind a leader and waddles through the house, quacking in rhythm — two steps, quack, two steps, quack. Change the leader often; every new leader gets to set the quack speed, and counting the steps sneaks in the maths.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the duck say? What does the baby say? Show me how a duck walks." The sharp quack, the tiny peep and the side-to-side waddle — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The peep-versus-quack contrast is the game that keeps giving — whisper-baby and shout-grown-up is volume control in disguise. At the pond, keep the watching at arm’s length: wild ducks are look-at animals, and the best pond visit ends with dry shoes.

    Staying safe

    Pond edges are the hazard: hold hands near the water, stay behind railings where there are any, and let the quacking happen from a safe step back. Wild ducks get watched, not chased — chasing scares them, and the water is deeper than it looks.

    This lesson pairs with the Duck flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Chicken — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson follows the busiest bird on the farm. Cluck is a small, busy sound — bok, bok, bok — and the hen on the card comes with two stories your child already eats: eggs at breakfast and the loudest alarm clock on the farm.

    What is this?

    A chicken is a farm bird that pecks at the ground all day, scratches for seeds and lays eggs. The card shows a hen — a grown-up chicken with a red comb on her head — and her busy chatter gets copied by people as cluck.

    What does it mean?

    Cluck is our copy of the hen’s busy sound. A hen clucks almost non-stop, chatting to keep her flock in touch the way families call from room to room. A rooster — the other kind of chicken — takes the loud morning shift instead: one enormous crow to start the day.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the hen’s sound is written cluck in English, hens lay the eggs we eat, the red bit on her head is called a comb, and the rooster’s job is the dawn crow — cock-a-doodle-doo — while the hen does the all-day talking.

    Why this matters

    Cluck is the perfect busy-person sound: small, repeated, rhythmic. Copying it paces speech like a drum, and the egg story gives your child an answer to a question they have wondered about — where does breakfast come from? — since their first bite of scrambled egg.

    What it teaches

    Rhythmic repetition (bok-bok-bok as speech pacing), animal role vocabulary (hen, rooster, chick), the food story of eggs, fine head-movement control in the pecking game, and sorting sounds by who makes them.

    Words to learn

    chickenhencluckeggpeckcomb

    Say this to your child

    “"The hen says cluck! Cluck, cluck, bok bok bok — she talks all day long, busy busy! Hens lay the eggs we eat for breakfast. And the rooster? He saves one huge shout for the morning: COCK-A-DOODLE-DOO! Can you be the hen… and now the rooster?"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the white bird says. Offer the real thing: cluck, cluck — bok, bok, bok — busy as a hen.
    2. Say the pair — the hen says cluck — and make it busy: small fast sounds, one after another, like tiny conversation.
    3. Look at the picture: this hen is white, with a red comb on her head. Point out the comb — every hen wears one, and no other farm bird does.
    4. Tell the egg story: hens lay eggs, eggs get collected each morning, and some of them become breakfast. An egg in the fridge is the exhibit A.
    5. Play the pecking game: quick head-nod pecks, one after another, while the clucking runs — then swap to the rooster for one giant cock-a-doodle-doo, hands as wings.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the hen? What sits on top of her head? What word is written with her? Does she look busy or sleepy?

    Ask your child

    "What does the hen say?" "What do we eat that hens give us?" "Who shouts in the morning — the hen or the rooster?" "Can you cluck and peck at the same time?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may cluck through every breakfast that features eggs, explain the comb to a puzzled grandparent, or deliver one room-shaking rooster crow at dawn — technically hours late for the job, artistically on target.

    Out in the real world

    Hens live at farms and city allotments alike, and eggs sit in nearly every fridge. The walk from hen to egg to breakfast plate is a food story short enough for a three-year-old to hold in one hand.

    Try it together

    The peck-and-cluck relay: scatter a few dry cereal pieces on a tray, and your child must move them one by one to a bowl — pecking with quick head-bobs, clucking all the while. It is fine-motor work, rhythm practice and chicken theatre, and the prize is the snack itself.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the hen say? What do we eat that she lays? Who does the giant morning shout?" The busy cluck, the egg and one huge crow — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Alternate hen-mode and rooster-mode on request — tiny busy sounds, then one giant one — because the contrast is the game and the volume control is the hidden lesson. A real egg carton makes the story tangible: shake it gently, name what laid it, cook it together.

    Staying safe

    Real hens at a farm get watched from the gate and touched only when the farmer says so — pecking is for pretend, and wash hands after any animal contact.

    This lesson pairs with the Chicken flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Horse — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson rides out with the tallest animal on the cards. Neigh starts high and falls away — a sound your child can ride — and the hooves underneath it supply the clip-clop beat that turns the whole house into a stable.

    What is this?

    A horse is a big, strong animal that people ride and drive. It stands on long legs, eats grass and hay, and has a loud sliding voice: the call people write as neigh — a whinny, in grown-up words.

    What does it mean?

    Neigh is our copy of a horse’s call: a squealy, sliding sound that starts at the top and falls to the bottom. A horse calls like this to find its friends across a field — a loud where-are-you? — and the hooves answer from far away with a clip-clop.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the horse’s sound is written neigh in English, horses carry riders and pull carts, their feet are called hooves and they go clip-clop, and a horse’s mane is the long hair on its neck that blows when it runs.

    Why this matters

    The neigh is a two-skill sound: a slide from high to low trains pitch control, and the clip-clop that goes with it trains rhythm. Together they are a mini music lesson wearing a horse costume — plus the gallop, which is gross-motor gold at this age.

    What it teaches

    Pitch control (high to low sliding), rhythm and steady beat in the clip-clop games, gross-motor galloping, animal vocabulary (mane, hooves, rider), and expressive loudness with a soft ending built in.

    Words to learn

    horseneighhoovesgallopmanerider

    Say this to your child

    “"The horse says neigh! Nnnneigh — start up high, slide all the way down. Neigh is our word for the horse’s big call. And listen underneath: clip-clop, clip-clop, those are the hooves! Climb on my back, we are going for a ride — clip-clop, clip-clop!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the tall animal says. Then give the slide: nnnneigh, starting high and coming down like a slide.
    2. Say the pair — the horse says neigh — and slide it together, high to low, two or three times. The fall at the end is the fun.
    3. Look at the picture: a brown horse standing tall. Trace the mane down its neck and count the four legs standing on the ground.
    4. Add the rhythm section: click your tongue for clip-clop, tap your knees in the same beat, then trot your fingers across the table.
    5. Gallop: one foot leads, the other chases, clip-clopping around the rug. A whole lap is the finish line — then a slow, proud walk back to the stable.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the horse? Where does the long hair grow — on its neck? What word sits with the horse? Do its legs look long or short?

    Ask your child

    "What does the horse say?" "Which way does the neigh slide — up or down?" "What sound do the hooves make?" "What does a horse eat?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may neigh down the slide at the playground, clip-clop through every hallway on two legs, or ask for a shoulder-ride with the promise of being the rider this time — sound, beat and gallop all in the stable now.

    Out in the real world

    Horses appear at riding schools, city police mounts, farms and fairs — often with hooves audible before the animal is visible. Each clip-clop you hear is the rhythm game inviting itself along, and each field of horses is a neigh contest waiting.

    Try it together

    Clip-clop parade: you are the horse, your child is the rider, and the route loops the sofa. Rider’s job: keep the beat going — pat-pat on your shoulders in rhythm. Swap roles so your child gallops and you ride. The beat belongs to whoever is ridden, which is funnier than it sounds.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the horse say? Which way does it slide? What do the hooves say?" The falling neigh, the answer and a confident clip-clop — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    Model the slide with your hand — high fingers falling to low — because the visual makes the pitch drop clickable. And keep the gallop on rugs and grass: hard floors are trotting country. The knee-tap beat is the quiet version for restaurants and waiting rooms.

    Staying safe

    Real horses are ridden or fed only with a grown-up in charge — those long legs move fast, and a horse’s height is exactly why small children meet them from the fence side, with permission.

    This lesson pairs with the Horse flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Pig — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson follows the nose. Oink is the only animal sound in the set that comes out upside down — squeezed up through the snout instead of out of the mouth — and your child is about to discover that their own nose can talk.

    What is this?

    A pig is a round, clever farm animal with a snout made for sniffing. It snuffles the ground for food, chats to its pig friends, and makes a grunt-snort that people copied as oink — the silliest honest word in the whole set.

    What does it mean?

    Oink is our copy of a pig’s grunt: a sniffy, snorty noise made with the nose, not the mouth. Try it and you feel the difference — the sound sneaks up from nowhere and comes out in a burst. Pigs talk like this while they work, and their work is smelling: the snout is the tool that finds dinner underground.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the pig’s sound is written oink in English, the snout is how pigs root out their food — a super-powered nose — and pigs are among the cleverest animals on the farm. The mud they love is not mess: it keeps them cool on hot days, like a bath that never dries.

    Why this matters

    Oink is a nose-sound, and nose-sounds are rare in speech practice — making one is a genuinely new motor trick. The snout story also flips a common insult: pigs are clean, smart and chatty, and a child who learns that early has picked up a little fairness along with the noise.

    What it teaches

    Oral-nasal control (sounds made with the nose — genuinely novel for speech), scent games and attention, animal fact-checking against old stories, and the giggle reflex that makes new sounds worth repeating.

    Words to learn

    pigoinksnoutsnufflegruntmud

    Say this to your child

    “"The pig says oink! Oink, oink — straight from the nose, not the mouth! Feel that? Pigs snuffle the ground with their snouts to find food, talking the whole time. And here is a secret: pigs are clean and clever — the mud is just their way of keeping cool. Sniff, sniff, OINK!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the pink animal says. Then demonstrate the nose-sound: a sniff-sniff and a snort — oink!
    2. Say the pair — the pig says oink — and let your child hunt for where the sound comes from: mouth or nose? (Nose. It surprises everyone.)
    3. Look at the picture: a smiling pink pig. Point to the snout — that big nose is the pig’s toolbox for finding food.
    4. Tell the honest mud story: pigs wallow to keep cool because they cannot sweat. The mud is their air-conditioning, not their mess.
    5. Play the snuffle game: hide a toy under a blanket and let your child snuffle for it, oinking on the approach like a pig on a mission.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the pig? Where is it smiling? What word sits with the pig? Can you find the big nose — the snout — in the picture?

    Ask your child

    "What does the pig say?" "Which part of the pig finds its food?" "Where does the oink come from — your mouth or your nose?" "Why do pigs like mud?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may snort-laugh through dinner, sniff out hidden objects with theatrical snuffling, or defend pigs hotly when a storybook calls them dirty — clean, clever and cool, thank you very much.

    Out in the real world

    Pigs appear at farms, in storybooks and as piggy banks on the dresser. The snout fact shows up anywhere food is found by smell — truffle pigs, airport detector dogs doing the same job — and your child now knows the whole snout trade.

    Try it together

    Snuffle treasure hunt: hide three small toys around one room, then let your child pig-walk to find them — sniffing the air, oinking on approach, snorting on discovery. Swap roles and be the pig yourself; getting out-snuffled by a three-year-old is the best part of the game.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the pig say? Where does the sound come from? What does the snout find?" The nose-made oink, the answer and one proud snort — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    If the oink will not come at first, have your child hum with their nose pinched, then release — the nose-sound arrives in one surprise. Keep the mud facts ready for storybook moments: correcting a pig slander is a language lesson as much as an animal one.

    This lesson pairs with the Pig flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Lion — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson opens the gate to the wild side. The roar is the biggest sound your child will copy all year — and the card’s friendly lion with the shaggy mane is the perfect king for it, roaring bravely from the safety of the rug.

    What is this?

    A lion is a huge wild cat with a shaggy mane around its face — the king of its grassland. Its voice is the biggest call in the set: a roar that thunders across the plains, copied by people as ROOOAR.

    What does it mean?

    Roar is our copy of the lion’s thunder. A real roar is so loud it rolls across whole valleys — the lion’s way of announcing here I am to every ear in reach. Your child’s roar carries across the living room, which is exactly the right size for a three-year-old lion.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the lion’s sound is written roar in English, lions are wild animals — admired from far away, never kept as pets — the shaggy collar of hair is called a mane, and a roar means the same thing every time: here I am.

    Why this matters

    The roar gives big feelings a safe outlet, and the whisper-roar that follows teaches the other half: volume control. Loud and soft in one game is emotional regulation in costume — the roar lets the feeling out, the whisper puts it away, on purpose, with a grin.

    What it teaches

    Breath power and sustained voicing, volume control (full roar to cub whisper), dramatic play with roles, wild-animal awareness — lions live in savannas, not houses — and the confidence of the loudest sound in the collection.

    Words to learn

    lionroarmanewildloudwhisper

    Say this to your child

    “"The lion says ROOOAR! Start small, grow big, let it thunder! A roar is the lion’s way of saying here I am — hear me! And the shaggy hair around his face is his mane, the king’s crown. Now show me your cub roar — so small only I can hear it. Perfect. Back to full roar!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and let your child meet the king: who is this, with the big shaggy hair? Then ask the question the whole card exists for: what does he say?
    2. Roar together — paws up, big breath, ROOOAR — starting soft and ending loud, the way a real roar builds.
    3. Look at the picture: the lion in the picture, mane all shaggy around his face. Explain the mane — only boy lions wear one, like a built-in crown.
    4. Play the volume dial: full roar, half roar, tiny cub roar, whisper roar. Every level is a different answer to the same here-I-am.
    5. Set the wild fact honestly: lions live far away on grassy plains, and we roar about them from the rug. Card lions roar; real lions stay wild.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the lion? Where does the shaggy mane grow — around the face? What word sits with the lion? Does he look friendly or fierce?

    Ask your child

    "What does the lion say?" "What is the shaggy hair called?" "How does a cub roar — big or small?" "Where do real lions live?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may greet every morning with a full royal roar, whisper-roar during quiet time without being asked, or explain to a visitor that only daddies have manes — volume control, wild facts and family mapping in one.

    Out in the real world

    Lions live at zoos and in storybooks, on flags and football badges. The wild fact travels with every sighting: we watch, we admire, we roar about it at home — and the roar means the same thing on the rug as it does on the plains.

    Try it together

    The volume dial: draw a big dial from 1 to 5 on paper. Your child roars at whatever number you point to — 1 is a sleeping-cub whisper, 5 is king-of-the-grassland. Add the reverse climb for challenge. It is the clearest volume-control game there is, and lions make it worth playing.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the lion say? What is his crown of hair called? Show me a whisper roar and a full roar." The mane, the range and the royal breath — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    End every roar session on the whisper — leaving the dial at two makes bedtime possible and quietly teaches that big voices have a small setting. If roars migrate to restaurants, the dial game compresses into one raised eyebrow: level one, cub.

    Staying safe

    Lions are wild animals: they live in zoos and on plains, watched from outside the enclosure, never approached or called to. Our roars stay friendly and our ears stay happy — a roar at full volume straight into someone’s face is a level five nobody asked for.

    This lesson pairs with the Lion flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Elephant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson trumpets in the giant. The elephant is the biggest animal walking the earth, its sound does not even come from its mouth — it blasts from the trunk — and the arm-trunk game that teaches it is the silliest thing your living room will host this month.

    What is this?

    An elephant is the biggest animal that walks on land, with ears like maps and a nose long enough to need its own name: the trunk. Its sound blasts out of that trunk — an airy Pbbbfft — and people copied it as a trumpet call.

    What does it mean?

    Trumpet is our copy of the elephant’s call: an airy blast through a long nose. And the trumpet is only half the story — elephants also rumble so deep that our ears can barely catch it, a secret voice that travels through the ground to far-away elephant feet. Loud and quiet, one animal.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the elephant’s blast is written as a trumpet in English, the trunk is a nose and a hand in one — it breathes, smells, sprays water and picks things up — the big ears help keep the giant cool, and the hidden rumble is the elephant’s quiet way of talking.

    Why this matters

    The trumpet is comic and physical — your child will love it — but the trunk idea is the real prize: a nose that works like an arm stretches what a body part can be, and that kind of flexible thinking is exactly what imagination is made of.

    What it teaches

    Gross-motor swing in the arm-trunk game, breath control for the blast, body-part flexibility (a nose that is also a hand), the biggest-animal superlative, and listening for sounds that are almost too low to hear.

    Words to learn

    elephanttrumpettrunkearsstompgiant

    Say this to your child

    “"The elephant says Pbbbfft! Trumpet through the trunk — the biggest nose in the world! The trunk breathes, smells, sprays water and picks up peanuts, all in one. Swing your arm-trunk with me… and blast! And here is the secret: elephants also rumble deeper than our ears can follow. Stomp, stomp — hello, says the giant."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask which animal is the biggest one on all the cards. Then introduce the giant and its strange nose: the trunk.
    2. Make the trumpet: take a big breath, let it rip through closed-ish lips — Pbbbfft! It comes out of the nose-end, just like a real trunk.
    3. Look at the picture: a gray giant with its ears spread wide. Trace the trunk from face to tip and flap your hands beside your own ears to feel how the big ears work.
    4. Play arm-trunk: swing one arm past your nose like a long trunk and let the blast rip as it swings high. Repeat until the room is fully elephant.
    5. Finish with the secret: elephants also rumble too low for our ears, talking through the ground. Stomp-stomp together — that is the elephant’s quiet half.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the elephant? How big are its ears compared to its head? What word sits with the elephant? Where does the trunk end?

    Ask your child

    "What does the elephant say?" "What is the long nose called?" "What can a trunk do that our nose cannot?" "How do elephants talk when the trumpet is off?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may trumpet at the bathtub with alarming accuracy, walk with one arm fixed as a permanent trunk, or stomp deliberately around the rug and announce "that is my quiet elephant talking" — sound, body and secret all in use.

    Out in the real world

    Elephants live at zoos and in storybooks and documentaries. Zoo trips gain a new layer — watch the trunk pick up a leaf, an ear flap in the heat — and the biggest-land-animal fact makes every elephant sighting feel like meeting a celebrity.

    Try it together

    Arm-trunk parade: one arm locked in front of the nose, the blast on every third step, stomp-stomp-TRUMPET across the room. Add a water hole where everyone kneels and slurps loudly through the trunk, then sprays. It is ridiculous, physical and impossible to do without laughing.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the elephant say? What is the long nose called and what can it do? What is the elephant’s secret quiet sound?" The blast, the trunk and the rumble — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The trumpet takes a few tries — loose lips, big breath, no shame. Model a bad one first and the pressure disappears. Keep the rumble as the bedtime chapter: the idea that a giant animal has a whisper voice is the gentlest thought in the whole set.

    Staying safe

    Real elephants are wild giants: watched from zoo paths and never touched outside farmer-or-keeper supervised moments. Their size that delights on a card is genuinely dangerous at arm’s length — the fence line is the rule, even for the friendliest giant.

    This lesson pairs with the Elephant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Frog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson takes a running hop at the smallest far-jumper in the collection. Ribbit is short and bouncy — one bounce per syllable — and the frog on the card brings the best transformation story going: from tadpole to hop.

    What is this?

    A frog is a small green jumper that lives near water, catching bugs with a tongue quicker than a blink. Its call is a short bouncy croak, and people copied the most famous version as ribbit — a word with a hop built into every syllable.

    What does it mean?

    Ribbit is our copy of one kind of frog — and different frogs croak differently all over the world, which makes ribbit the local accent of frog. What every version shares is the bounce: the sound and the hop arrive together, as if the call itself were jumping.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the frog’s sound is written ribbit in English, frogs hop instead of walk, they catch bugs with a sticky tongue, and they grow up in the water — starting as tadpoles, tiny swimming dots, before legs arrive and the hopping starts.

    Why this matters

    The frog carries the set’s best growing-up story: egg, tadpole, frog. It is transformation a child can follow start to finish, and it quietly teaches that babies can look nothing like their parents — a fact your child will later recognize in butterflies, and, in small ways, in themselves.

    What it teaches

    Gross-motor hopping and landing, the tadpole-to-frog sequence, imitation of a staccato sound, pond-life vocabulary, and patience — the transformation takes months, which is a long time by three-year-old measures.

    Words to learn

    frogribbithoppondcroaktadpole

    Say this to your child

    “"The frog says ribbit! Ribbit, ribbit — one hop for every ribbit! Ribbit is our copy of the frog’s call, and frogs croak it all around the world, each pond with its own accent. Before the hopping, the frog was a tadpole — a tiny swimmer with a tail. Wiggle, wiggle… legs! Hop, hop, RIBBIT!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the green jumper says. Then demonstrate: ribbit, ribbit — with a hop on each one.
    2. Say the pair — the frog says ribbit — and keep the bounce rule: no ribbit without a hop. Sound and jump, locked together.
    3. Look at the picture: a green frog sitting on its front legs, folded and ready. Fold yourself into the same shape — squat low, hands down, coiled like a spring.
    4. Tell the growing story: frog eggs hatch into tadpoles that swim like tiny fish, then legs grow, the tail shrinks away, and one day the pond has a jumper. Act it: wiggle small, then hop big.
    5. Hold a hop-and-ribbit race across the rug: one hop, one ribbit, all the way. Frogs rest between jumps — so do racers.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: what color is the frog? Where are its front legs — is it sitting on them? What word sits with the frog? Do its back legs look ready to jump?

    Ask your child

    "What does the frog say?" "What was the frog before it was a frog?" "How does a frog move — walking or hopping?" "What does a frog eat, and how does its tongue help?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may ribbit-hop the entire length of the hallway, explain the tadpole story in reverse to a confused teddy, or crouch folded like the card and wait, coiled, for someone to say go — the shape, sound and story all jumped into one.

    Out in the real world

    Frogs live at ponds, streams and damp gardens — and after spring rain, the whole neighbourhood croaks. A puddle-side visit at dusk is the real-life soundtrack; frogspawn in a pond in spring is the growing story happening live.

    Try it together

    Tadpole-to-frog transformation: start curled and wiggling on the floor — egg, then tadpole, swimming tiny circles. Then legs! Hop up, ribbit, and you are frogs. Run it slowly with narration, then speed it up until the transformation takes three seconds and everyone collapses laughing.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the frog say? What was it before? Show me a hop with a ribbit." The bounce, the tadpole and one springy jump — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The no-hop-no-ribbit rule is what makes the game — it fuses sound to movement and doubles the exercise. If real frogs appear at the pond, watch from the bank: frogs’ skins are delicate, and the best frog is an observed frog.

    Staying safe

    Pond banks are slippery and frog hunts stay on the dry side of the edge — small frogs get looked at, gently, and hands get washed after any pond touching.

    This lesson pairs with the Frog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR SOUNDS · AGES 3–4 YEARS

    Bird — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson closes the set with the tiniest voice and the biggest reach. Tweet is our word for the little high calls birds sing — and it is the only animal sound in the collection your child can hear live, free, from the kitchen window.

    What is this?

    A bird is the animal everyone can hear from the window: wings, feathers, and a voice far bigger than its body. Birds sing many different songs, and people copy the little high ones as tweet — the smallest sound in the whole set.

    What does it mean?

    Tweet is our copy of a bird’s tiny high notes — but no two birds sing exactly alike, which makes tweet the umbrella word for a whole chorus. Real tweets come in twiddles and trills; the word is the simple version, like a stick drawing of a wave.

    What does the child need to know?

    Your child needs to know: the little high bird sounds are written tweet in English, birds sing with their throats and fly with their wings, they live in nests and sing most at sunrise, and the real thing is available outside — ears ready.

    Why this matters

    The bird gives animal sounds their grand finale: the step from card to world. Every other voice needed imagination; this one needs only a window and a quiet minute. Hearing a real tweet and matching it to the word is the moment the whole collection becomes true.

    What it teaches

    Quiet listening — a genuinely hard skill at three, and a foundational one — matching heard sounds to words, bird and nature vocabulary, sunrise-and-nesting science at a gentle level, and the stillness that lets wild things come near.

    Words to learn

    birdtweetwingssingnestlisten

    Say this to your child

    “"The bird says tweet! Tweet, tweet — the tiniest voice on all our cards. Tweet is our word for the little high sounds birds sing. Now the brave part: be as quiet as a statue, ears open, and let us count the real tweets outside. One… two… you just met a bird in person."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and ask what the little bluebird says. Offer the smallest voice in the set: tweet, tweet — high and tiny.
    2. Say the pair — the bird says tweet — and make it tiny: pinch the sound high and small, three or four quick notes.
    3. Look at the picture: the little bluebird, one wing lifted in a wave. Wave back, then flap both arms and ask what wings are for.
    4. Play the listening minute: sit by the window or step outside, get as quiet as statues, and raise one finger for every tweet heard. Two fingers is a triumph.
    5. Finish with the nest story: birds build nests, lay eggs, and sing to greet the morning — which is why the day starts with birdsong whether we are up or not.

    Look closer at the picture

    Look at the picture together: how tiny is this bird — small enough for a hand? What color are its feathers? Which wing is lifted — is it waving? What word sits with the bird?

    Ask your child

    "What does the bird say?" "What do birds use their wings for?" "Where do birds sleep and lay their eggs?" "How quiet do we have to be to hear a real tweet?"

    What your child can say or do

    Your child may hold a finger up in absolute silence and whisper "one tweet!", sing morning tweets from bed before any words arrive, or announce every garden bird with proprietary delight — the smallest card, the proudest owner.

    Out in the real world

    Birds deliver the lesson daily and free: the dawn chorus, pigeons in the square, sparrows at the bus stop. Each tweet heard out loud is a repetition no flashcard can match — and each one lands on a child who now has the word for it.

    Try it together

    The listening minute: same time each day, one quiet minute by the window or on the step, counting tweets on raised fingers. Keep a tally with a sticker for every bird minute — the quiet is the practice, and the streak is the motivation.

    Understanding check

    Ask: "What does the bird say? What are wings for? How do we find out if a real bird is singing?" The tiny high tweet, the flying and one finger held up — that is the lesson landed.

    Parent tips

    The listening minute works best with a grown-up being quiet too — your stillness is the permission for theirs. If no tweets appear, any bird sound counts: coos, caws, chirps are all bird voices, and your child will happily name them all tweets for now.

    Staying safe

    Bird watching happens with eyes and ears: birds stay wild, nests stay untouched, and chicks on the ground get reported to a grown-up rather than rescued by small hands.

    This lesson pairs with the Bird flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Sounds.
